lesson.title: Protons in Motion: The Basics of Acids and Bases
lesson.summary: Acids donate hydrogen ions and bases accept them, and because water itself can act as both, this proton-transfer chemistry drives an enormous share of the reactions happening inside living cells.
lesson.body:
An acid, by the definition most useful in biology, is any substance that donates a hydrogen ion, a proton, to another substance, while a base is any substance that accepts one. This is called the Bronsted-Lowry definition, and it works well for water chemistry because a water molecule's covalent bonds, the very bonds whose uneven electron sharing make water polar, can break in a way that releases a proton to a neighboring molecule.

Water itself is not chemically inert; a small fraction of water molecules are constantly reacting with each other. One water molecule donates a proton to a neighboring water molecule, producing a hydronium ion, written H3O+, and leaving behind a hydroxide ion, OH-. This process, called the autoionization of water, happens in both directions simultaneously and reaches a stable equilibrium in pure water where the concentrations of H3O+ and OH- are equal and quite small. Because water can both donate and accept a proton, chemists describe it as amphoteric, able to act as either an acid or a base depending on what it reacts with.

Acids and bases differ enormously in how readily they give up or take on protons. Strong acids like hydrochloric acid essentially dissociate completely in water, releasing nearly all of their protons to become H3O+ and chloride ions. Weak acids, by contrast, only partially dissociate, existing in a dynamic equilibrium between the intact molecule and its dissociated ions. Acetic acid, the acid in vinegar, is a familiar weak acid, and this same weak-acid behavior appears throughout biochemistry: the carboxyl groups found on amino acids and fatty acids only partially release their protons in water, which is exactly why their behavior depends so heavily on the surrounding pH.

This chemistry operates constantly inside living tissue. The stomach lining secretes hydrochloric acid to create an extremely acidic environment that activates digestive enzymes and kills many ingested pathogens. Blood carries dissolved carbon dioxide largely in the form of carbonic acid, which can donate a proton to become bicarbonate, a reaction that runs in both directions depending on how much carbon dioxide the body needs to expel through the lungs. Every one of these systems depends on the same underlying behavior described above, molecules donating and accepting protons, playing out at a massive physiological scale. Even something as simple as lemon juice tasting sour reflects this chemistry: citric acid molecules in the juice partially dissociate in the watery saliva on your tongue, releasing free protons that sour taste receptors detect directly.

Because the concentration of free hydrogen ions in a solution determines how acidic or basic it is, and because that concentration governs the shape and function of proteins, nucleic acids, and enzymes, quantifying it precisely became essential to chemistry and biology alike. That need for a precise, standardized way to describe acidity is exactly what the pH scale was built to solve.
